blocks.text: COVID-19 (**coronavirus disease 2019**) is caused by **SARS-CoV-2**, a **novel coronavirus** first recognised in **December 2019** during an outbreak of severe respiratory illness in **Wuhan, China**. It spread around the world within months to become a **pandemic**, and new **variants of concern** keep appearing.

blocks.title: Virology in brief
items: Coronaviruses are **enveloped RNA viruses** with **helical** symmetry, roughly **80–220 nm** across.
They infect **animals as well as humans**; SARS-CoV and MERS-CoV are zoonoses, and Kumar & Clark also lists COVID-19 in its zoonosis table (source uncertain).
Human members: the seasonal **229E, OC43, NL63 and HKU1**, plus **SARS-CoV, MERS-CoV and SARS-CoV-2**.
SARS-CoV-2 is grouped with the viral causes of **atypical community-acquired pneumonia**, alongside influenza A/B, adenovirus, parainfluenza and RSV.

blocks.title: Human coronaviruses compared
rows: Common cold (short, mild upper respiratory infection)
Severe lower respiratory infection with bronchopneumonia; about 8000 cases, ~10% died
Severe pneumonia, ARDS, renal failure; mortality about 35%
COVID-19: asymptomatic to ARDS and multi-organ failure; early mortality estimate 1–5%

blocks.text: SARS-CoV-2 is a textbook **emerging infectious disease**, like MERS-CoV, Zika and Ebola. Many emerging pathogens are **zoonoses**, helped along by population movement, global travel and trade, ecological and climate change, and changes in farming.

"Coronavirus" does not always mean severe disease. The **seasonal coronaviruses** behave like rhinovirus and cause brief, mild colds; only **SARS-CoV, MERS-CoV and SARS-CoV-2** cause life-threatening lower respiratory infection.

The **animal reservoir of SARS-CoV-2 is unproven**. Kumar & Clark’s zoonosis table tentatively suggests snakes or pangolins, but marks it as uncertain, so do not state it as fact. By contrast, SARS most likely came from **bats** and MERS from **camels**. The Davidson’s text used here has no COVID-19 section.

blocks.title: How SARS-CoV-2 spreads
items: Mainly **person to person** through **respiratory droplets and particles**, especially at **close range**.
Kumar & Clark lists COVID-19 as a **zoonosis** whose onward spread between people is by **droplets**.
People who are **asymptomatic or pre-symptomatic** can pass the virus on.
It is far **more transmissible than the original SARS-CoV**, though less lethal, which explains its explosive worldwide spread.
General routes for respiratory pathogens: **inhalation**, **direct contact**, and **fomites** (door handles, taps, ultrasound probes), which matter most in health care–associated infection.
For coronaviruses as a cause of colds, infectivity peaks **early in the illness**, via droplets or nasal secretions carried on the hands.

blocks.text: Because **pre-symptomatic and asymptomatic** people shed the virus, isolating only those with symptoms will miss cases. This is why distancing, masks and hand hygiene are applied to everyone during spread.
Do not quote the **2–7 day** figure for COVID-19; that is the incubation of the **2003 SARS coronavirus**. For SARS-CoV-2 remember **up to 14 days, typically around 5**.

Infection ranges from **completely asymptomatic** to life-threatening. Among symptomatic patients about **81% have mild-to-moderate**, **14% severe** (hypoxic) and **5% critical** disease (ARDS, shock, multi-organ failure). Severe disease reflects an **exaggerated host inflammatory response** (cytokine storm syndrome) causing fever, multi-organ dysfunction, cardiac and renal injury, and ARDS.

blocks.title: Symptoms
items: **Fever** and chills
Upper respiratory symptoms: **cough**, **sore throat**, nasal congestion
**Breathlessness** in more serious disease
**Myalgia** and **headache**
**Loss of smell (anosmia)** and **loss of taste (ageusia)**, which are common and characteristic
Gastrointestinal: **nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea**

blocks.title: Risk factors for severe illness
items: **Age ≥ 65** (advanced age)
Cardiovascular disease and previous **stroke**
**Diabetes mellitus**
Chronic **lung disease** and **chronic kidney disease**
**Obesity** and **cancer**
Low socioeconomic status

blocks.title: Investigations
rows: **Most sensitive** test; **nasopharyngeal swab** is the most reliable specimen (lower respiratory or anterior nasal samples can also be used)
Anterior nasal swab; **less sensitive than PCR** but gives a point-of-care result so the patient can isolate sooner
**Lymphopenia** (the most common lab abnormality) and thrombocytopenia
Raised **D-dimer**, **CRP**/ESR, **LDH**, ALT/AST and creatinine, mostly in hospitalised patients
Multifocal bilateral **peripheral ground-glass opacities**, often in the **posterior lower lobes**, with consolidation and air bronchograms

blocks.note: Look at: CT of COVID-19 pneumonia with dense opacities in both lower lobes and air bronchograms.

blocks.text: **Lymphopenia, thrombocytopenia and a raised LDH** appear among the lab changes of hospitalised COVID-19, and Davidson lists exactly this trio for MERS, so the pattern is worth recognising across the severe coronaviruses.

A **negative rapid antigen test** or a **normal early chest X-ray** does not exclude COVID-19. Antigen tests are less sensitive than PCR, and the X-ray may lag behind the illness; CT helps when the diagnosis is uncertain.

blocks.title: Complications by system
rows: **Acute hypoxic respiratory failure**, sometimes **without breathlessness** ("silent hypoxia"); **ARDS**
**Shock** and multi-organ dysfunction syndrome; cardiac injury from the inflammatory response
Higher risk of **stroke** and other neurological complications; COVID-19 is a recognised trigger of **Guillain–Barré syndrome**
**AKI in about 17% of inpatients**, usually **ATN**, less often **collapsing FSGS** (high-risk APOL1 genotype); dialysis circuits clot more readily
Acute mild-to-moderate **aminotransferase rise** (under 15 × the upper limit of normal)

blocks.title: Severity of the three serious coronaviruses
rows: About 8000 cases, ~800 deaths; no natural cases since 2003
Over 2200 cases, mostly in the Middle East; the largest outbreaks spread within health-care settings
Nearly 5 million cases and 300,000 deaths by May 2020

blocks.text: **Silent hypoxia**: a patient with COVID-19 can be markedly hypoxic yet not feel breathless, so asking about dyspnoea alone can miss respiratory failure.

SARS-CoV-2 is **less lethal per case** than SARS-CoV or MERS-CoV but caused far more deaths overall because it is **much more transmissible**. Kumar’s 1–5% mortality figure was an early-pandemic estimate, and Step-Up notes that later sequelae are still not fully characterised.

Care is **largely supportive**, with **supplemental oxygen** at its centre. Drug treatment is matched to severity and to whether the patient needs oxygen. Corticosteroids, antivirals such as remdesivir and monoclonal antibodies are used in **selected** patients.

blocks.title: Treatment ladder by severity
rows: Manage **at home**: isolation, monitoring and symptom relief (antipyretics, analgesics, antitussives, fluids)
Not hospitalised but at **high risk** of severe disease
Mechanical ventilation or ECMO (or oxygen needs rising fast before intubation)
Dexamethasone **plus** an **IL-6 blocker** (tocilizumab, sarilumab) **or** a **JAK inhibitor** (baricitinib, tofacitinib)
**Anticoagulation**: prophylactic or therapeutic dose chosen by severity and risk

blocks.title: Key drug facts
items: **Dexamethasone** lowers **28-day mortality** in patients receiving oxygen for COVID-19 pneumonia.
**Remdesivir** works by inhibiting the **viral RNA polymerase**.
IL-6 blockers and JAK inhibitors target the **inflammatory (cytokine storm)** phase, not the virus.
Severe cases need **inpatient care**; the older textbooks manage severe coronavirus pneumonia (MERS) supportively in an airborne infection isolation room.

blocks.text: The step that triggers **dexamethasone** is **needing oxygen**. Steroid benefit was shown in patients on oxygen, and the treatment ladder reserves it for hospitalised patients on supplemental O2 or more.

Davidson’s 24e and Kumar give **no COVID-specific drugs**; their only advice for severe coronavirus pneumonia is supportive care with isolation. The drug ladder above comes from US guideline-based quick sources and is **time-sensitive**, so follow your current course guidance for exact choices and doses.

blocks.title: COVID-19 vaccines
items: **Vaccination is the key prevention strategy.** Several formulations exist, including **mRNA vaccines**.
The vaccines target the viral **spike protein** and are highly effective.
Their main effect is to **reduce severity**: breakthrough infection still happens but is much milder.

First Aid (US guidance at the time of writing) recommends vaccination for **everyone aged 6 months and older**; dose number, spacing and boosters differ by manufacturer (e.g. Pfizer-BioNTech, Moderna, Janssen/J&J).
Particularly important for the **elderly** and those with **significant comorbidities**; listed alongside **influenza and pneumococcal** vaccines for pneumonia prevention.

blocks.title: General immunisation principles (Davidson)
rows: Vaccine of whole organisms (live attenuated or inactivated) or components (proteins, polysaccharides)
**Live vaccines** give T-cell and antibody responses and are more immunogenic than inactivated whole-cell vaccines, but are generally **avoided in the immunocompromised**
Ready-made antibodies given to the patient
Protection is **immediate but short** (weeks to months); carries the **risks of blood products**

blocks.text: Exam framing: COVID-19 vaccines **reduce severe disease** far more reliably than they prevent infection, so a vaccinated person with mild COVID-19 is a vaccine success, not a failure.

Vaccine products, age thresholds and booster schedules come from a fast-changing US schedule (First Aid gives them "at the time of writing", beside a 2021 CDC schedule). Learn the principles (spike-protein target, severity reduction, priority for older and comorbid patients) rather than brand-specific schedules.

blocks.title: Personal and community prevention
items: **Physical distancing** (about 6 feet) and avoiding crowds
**Mask** wearing
**Handwashing** or alcohol hand sanitiser, and less hand-to-face contact
Good indoor **ventilation**
Quarantine and isolation according to current public-health guidance

blocks.title: Isolation precautions (Davidson Box 6.9)
rows: Private room (or patients at least 1 m apart); **surgical mask** for staff in close contact
Private room preferred; **gloves and gown** for contact with the patient or contaminated areas
**Negative-pressure room** with air exhausted outside or filtered; **N95 respirators** for staff; avoid non-immune staff
Used for **SARS**, viral haemorrhagic fever, smallpox and adenovirus pneumonia

blocks.title: In the hospital
items: Staff caring for COVID-19 patients wear **gown, gloves and eye protection**; an **N95 mask is mandatory for aerosol-generating procedures**.
Severe coronavirus pneumonia (MERS) is managed in an **airborne infection isolation room** with contact and airborne precautions and full PPE.

**Hand hygiene** is the single most important IPC measure: before and after every patient contact; alcohol rub is usually enough, but use **soap and water** if hands are visibly soiled. A full wash takes **40–60 seconds**.
Follow the WHO **"Five Moments"** for hand hygiene and communicate infection status when transferring patients.
The wider IPC bundle: staff education, PPE, **immunisation of health workers**, environmental cleaning, specialised ventilation, surveillance and isolation.
Early symptoms are non-specific, so staff must stay alert; scrupulous infection control limited spread in the 2003 SARS outbreak.

blocks.title: Public health
items: COVID-19 is a **reportable disease**: clinicians must notify public-health authorities.
Davidson lists **SARS and MERS-CoV** as notifiable because they are novel or growing threats to health.
A **pandemic** is an epidemic spread over several countries or continents that affects a large share of the population.
Strong **surveillance** picks up emerging pathogens early and guides outbreak control.

blocks.note: Look at: the WHO hand-washing steps, and the areas most often missed (fingertips, web spaces, palmar creases, backs of hands).

blocks.text: A **surgical mask** is a droplet precaution. For **aerosol-generating procedures** (e.g. intubation) on a COVID-19 patient, staff need an **N95 respirator** plus gown, gloves and eye protection.

cards.front: Which virus causes COVID-19, and when and where was it first identified?
cards.back: **SARS-CoV-2**, a novel coronavirus, identified in **December 2019** in **Wuhan, China**.
**Enveloped RNA viruses** with helical symmetry, about 80–220 nm.

cards.front: Which three human coronaviruses cause life-threatening lower respiratory infection?

cards.back: Person to person through **respiratory droplets/particles** at close range; asymptomatic and pre-symptomatic spread occurs.

cards.front: Which loss-of-sense symptoms are common in COVID-19?
Most sensitive diagnostic test for COVID-19, and the best specimen?
Most common laboratory abnormality in hospitalised COVID-19?
cards.back: **Lymphopenia** (also thrombocytopenia, raised D-dimer, CRP, LDH, transaminases).

cards.front: Typical CT chest pattern in COVID-19 pneumonia?
cards.back: Bilateral, **peripheral ground-glass opacities**, often posterior lower lobes, with consolidation and air bronchograms.
**AKI in ~17% of inpatients**, mostly **ATN**; less often **collapsing FSGS** (APOL1 high-risk genotype).

cards.front: Which hospitalised COVID-19 patients get dexamethasone, and why?
cards.back: Those needing **supplemental oxygen** (or more); it **reduces 28-day mortality**.

cards.front: Target and main benefit of COVID-19 vaccines?
cards.back: Target the **spike protein**; mainly **reduce severity** (breakthrough infection is milder).

cards.front: PPE for an aerosol-generating procedure on a COVID-19 patient?
cards.back: **N95 respirator** plus gown, gloves and eye protection.

cards.front: Single most important infection prevention and control measure?
cards.back: **Hand hygiene**, before and after every patient contact.

questions.stem: A medical student is revising the 2019 outbreak of severe respiratory illness that began in Wuhan, China, and spread worldwide within months.
questions.leadIn: What type of organism is the causative agent?
options: Segmented negative-strand RNA virus of the orthomyxovirus family
Intracellular bacterium lacking a cell wall
questions.explanation: The agent is **SARS-CoV-2**, a coronavirus. Coronaviruses are **enveloped RNA viruses** with helical symmetry.
whyNot: Adenoviruses are non-enveloped DNA viruses; coronaviruses carry RNA and have an envelope.
This describes influenza, not a coronavirus.
This describes Mycoplasma, a cause of atypical pneumonia but not of COVID-19.
Fungi did not cause the 2019 pandemic.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man has 3 days of sneezing, a blocked nose and a mild sore throat. A respiratory viral panel detects coronavirus OC43. He is worried because he has heard coronaviruses cause pandemics.
questions.leadIn: What is the best description of this infection?
options: A short, mild upper respiratory infection like a rhinovirus cold
A notifiable infection needing airborne isolation
An early stage of severe acute respiratory syndrome
An infection likely to progress to ARDS within a week
questions.explanation: OC43 is a **seasonal coronavirus** that causes the **common cold**. Only SARS-CoV, MERS-CoV and SARS-CoV-2 cause life-threatening lower respiratory disease.
whyNot: Notification and enhanced isolation apply to the novel coronaviruses (SARS, MERS, COVID-19), not to seasonal OC43.
SARS is caused by SARS-CoV, a distinct virus that has not circulated naturally since 2003.
Camel contact is linked to MERS-CoV.
Seasonal coronaviruses cause self-limiting colds, not ARDS.

questions.stem: A household contact of a woman with confirmed COVID-19 asks how the virus mainly spreads.
questions.leadIn: What is the main route of transmission?
options: Respiratory droplets and particles during close contact
questions.explanation: SARS-CoV-2 spreads mainly **person to person** via **respiratory droplets/particles**, especially at close range.
whyNot: Faecal–oral spread is the route of enteric infections such as typhoid or norovirus.
Mosquitoes transmit malaria, dengue and Zika.
Blood-borne spread applies to HIV and hepatitis B/C.
Ingestion of undercooked meat is not how COVID-19 spreads; camel products are a MERS concern.

questions.stem: A nurse had close unprotected contact with a patient who was later confirmed to have COVID-19. She feels well 3 days after the exposure.
questions.leadIn: What is the typical incubation period of COVID-19?
questions.explanation: The incubation period is **2–14 days**, with an average of about **5 days** (median 4–5). Being well at day 3 does not exclude infection.
whyNot: Too short: this suits toxin-mediated food poisoning.
This is Davidson’s figure for the 2003 SARS coronavirus, not SARS-CoV-2.
Too long; this suits infections such as hepatitis A.
Far too long for any acute respiratory virus.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old teacher has 2 days of fever, dry cough and muscle aches. She says food tastes of nothing and she cannot smell coffee.
questions.leadIn: Which infection is most likely?
questions.explanation: **Anosmia and ageusia** with fever and cough are characteristic of **COVID-19**.
whyNot: Streptococcal pharyngitis causes a painful throat and exudate, not loss of smell and taste.
Glandular fever gives sore throat, lymphadenopathy and fatigue rather than anosmia.
Legionella causes severe pneumonia, often with confusion and GI upset, not anosmia.
TB has a subacute course with weight loss and night sweats.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man is admitted with fever, cough and hypoxia. A rapid antigen test is negative. COVID-19 is still suspected.
questions.leadIn: Which test is most sensitive for confirming the diagnosis?
options: Repeat rapid antigen test on a throat swab
questions.explanation: **NAAT (RT-PCR)** on a **nasopharyngeal** sample is the most sensitive test. Rapid antigen tests are quicker but less sensitive.
whyNot: Antigen testing is less sensitive than PCR whatever the site, so a negative result does not settle it.
D-dimer is often raised in COVID-19 but is non-specific and not diagnostic.
The X-ray may be normal early and its changes are not specific.
Blood cultures look for bacteraemia, not a respiratory virus.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old woman with COVID-19 is chatting comfortably on the ward and denies breathlessness. Her oxygen saturation is 86% on room air.
questions.leadIn: Which complication does this illustrate?
questions.explanation: COVID-19 can cause **acute hypoxic respiratory failure without breathlessness** ("silent hypoxia").
whyNot: PE is a recognised complication but typically presents with sudden breathlessness or pleuritic pain; nothing here points to it.
Hyperventilation does not cause a saturation of 86%.
GBS causes ascending weakness, not isolated hypoxia.
Nothing here suggests a new bacterial infection.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man admitted with severe COVID-19 develops a rising creatinine and falling urine output on day 6.
questions.leadIn: What is the most common renal lesion in COVID-19-associated AKI?
questions.explanation: COVID-associated AKI affects about **17% of inpatients** and is usually **ATN**; collapsing FSGS is less common.
whyNot: Collapsing FSGS occurs, mainly with a high-risk APOL1 genotype, but is less common than ATN.
Membranous nephropathy is not a typical COVID lesion.
Post-streptococcal GN follows streptococcal infection.
Renal artery stenosis is a chronic vascular lesion, not an acute viral complication.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man is admitted with COVID-19 pneumonia. His saturation is 89% on air and he is started on supplemental oxygen. He is not ventilated.
questions.leadIn: Which drug has been shown to reduce 28-day mortality in this situation?
questions.explanation: In patients needing **oxygen** for COVID-19 pneumonia, **dexamethasone** lowers 28-day mortality and is the backbone of inpatient treatment.
whyNot: Oseltamivir is a neuraminidase inhibitor for influenza.
Antibiotics do not treat the virus; there is no sign of bacterial infection.
IL-6 blockers are added to dexamethasone in ventilated patients or those deteriorating fast, not given instead of it.
Molnupiravir is an oral antiviral for high-risk patients who are not in hospital.

questions.stem: A pharmacology tutor asks how remdesivir acts against SARS-CoV-2.
questions.leadIn: What is its mechanism of action?
options: Inhibition of the viral RNA polymerase
Neutralisation of the spike protein by antibody
questions.explanation: **Remdesivir** inhibits the **viral RNA polymerase**, blocking viral replication.
whyNot: This is tocilizumab or sarilumab.
This is baricitinib or tofacitinib.
This is oseltamivir in influenza.
This describes neutralising monoclonal antibodies.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old woman with diabetes asks what COVID-19 vaccination mainly achieves.
questions.leadIn: What is the main benefit of vaccination?
options: It greatly reduces the severity of illness
It replaces the need for hand hygiene in hospitals
It works only if given within 48 hours of exposure
questions.explanation: COVID-19 vaccines target the **spike protein**. They are highly effective, mainly by **reducing severe illness**; breakthrough infections still occur but are milder.
whyNot: Breakthrough infection still occurs.
Vaccines prevent disease; they are not a treatment.
Hand hygiene remains the key IPC measure.
The 48-hour window applies to influenza antivirals, not vaccination.

questions.stem: A patient is given ready-made antibodies against a pathogen after an exposure.
questions.leadIn: Which statement about this type of immunisation is correct?
options: Protection is immediate but lasts only weeks to months
It produces lifelong memory T-cell immunity
It is a live attenuated vaccine
It must be avoided in all immunocompromised patients
It carries no risk because no blood products are involved
questions.explanation: This is **passive immunisation**: protection starts at once but lasts only **weeks to months**, and because the antibodies come from blood it carries **blood-product risks**.
whyNot: Lasting memory responses come from active immunisation.
Live attenuated vaccines are a form of active immunisation.
It is live vaccines, not antibodies, that are generally avoided in the immunocompromised.
The antibodies are derived from blood, so blood-product risks apply.

questions.stem: A junior doctor is about to intubate a patient with confirmed COVID-19.
questions.leadIn: Which respiratory protection is required?
options: No mask if gloves and gown are worn
questions.explanation: Intubation is an **aerosol-generating procedure**, so an **N95** respirator is mandatory, with gown, gloves and eye protection.
whyNot: A surgical mask is a droplet precaution and does not protect against aerosols.
Cloth coverings are a community measure, not health-care PPE.
Eye protection is needed as well as, not instead of, a respirator.
Gloves and gown do not protect the airway.

questions.stem: Hospital managers want to prioritise one measure to reduce health care–associated spread of respiratory viruses.
questions.leadIn: Which measure does Davidson rank most important?
options: Closing the hospital to visitors permanently
questions.explanation: Davidson names **good hand hygiene** as the most important IPC measure: before and after every patient contact, using alcohol rub, or soap and water if hands are visibly soiled.
whyNot: Antibiotics do nothing against viruses and promote resistance.
Chest X-ray screening is not an IPC measure for respiratory viruses.
This is not part of standard IPC measures.
Symptom checks miss pre-symptomatic spread and are not ranked first.

questions.stem: A healthy 25-year-old man had a mild cold-like illness and tested positive for SARS-CoV-2. He asks how his flatmate, who never had symptoms, could have infected him.
questions.leadIn: Which statement best explains this?
options: Asymptomatic and pre-symptomatic people can transmit SARS-CoV-2
SARS-CoV-2 spreads only from symptomatic patients
He must have caught it from an animal reservoir
Infection can only be acquired in hospitals
questions.explanation: SARS-CoV-2 can spread from people who are **asymptomatic or not yet symptomatic**, which is why symptom-based isolation alone is not enough.
whyNot: This is the misconception the question targets.
Spread is overwhelmingly person to person; the animal source is uncertain.
Community spread is the norm.
It is a respiratory, not blood-borne, infection.

questions.stem: A 67-year-old man with COVID-19 is admitted. Which blood result is the single most common laboratory abnormality in such patients?
questions.leadIn: Choose the most likely finding.
questions.explanation: **Lymphopenia** is the commonest lab abnormality in hospitalised COVID-19, often with thrombocytopenia and raised D-dimer, CRP and LDH.
whyNot: Neutrophilia suggests bacterial infection and is not the classic COVID-19 finding.
Eosinophilia points to parasites or allergy.
COVID-19 does not raise the haemoglobin.
Hypercalcaemia is not a recognised COVID-19 laboratory feature.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old woman with COVID-19 has a CT chest.
questions.leadIn: Which pattern is most typical?
options: Bilateral peripheral ground-glass opacities in the lower lobes
Unilateral lobar consolidation with a large pleural effusion
questions.explanation: CT typically shows **multifocal, bilateral, peripheral ground-glass opacities**, often **posterior lower lobe**, with consolidation and air bronchograms.
whyNot: Upper-lobe cavitation suggests tuberculosis.
Unilateral lobar consolidation with effusion suggests bacterial pneumonia.
Isolated hilar nodes suggest sarcoidosis or lymphoma.
Honeycombing indicates established pulmonary fibrosis.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man with COVID-19 is on dexamethasone and oxygen. Over 12 hours his oxygen needs rise sharply and he is moved to ICU, where he is intubated.
questions.leadIn: Which drug class should be added to dexamethasone?
options: An interleukin-6 receptor blocker such as tocilizumab
A second corticosteroid at high dose
An oral antiviral such as molnupiravir
questions.explanation: In ventilated patients (or those whose oxygen needs rise rapidly), **dexamethasone plus an IL-6 blocker** (tocilizumab, sarilumab) or a **JAK inhibitor** (baricitinib, tofacitinib) targets the inflammatory phase.
whyNot: Neuraminidase inhibitors treat influenza.
There is no evidence of fungal infection.
A second steroid is not part of the ladder.
Molnupiravir is for high-risk patients who are not in hospital.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old man admitted with COVID-19 develops sudden pleuritic chest pain, tachycardia and a further fall in saturation on day 9.
questions.leadIn: Which complication is most likely?
questions.explanation: COVID-19 carries a **high rate of thrombosis**, including **pulmonary embolism**, which is why inpatients are anticoagulated.
whyNot: SBP complicates ascites in cirrhosis.
Aortic stenosis is a chronic valve lesion.
Meningitis presents with headache, neck stiffness and fever.
Pancreatitis causes epigastric pain radiating to the back.

questions.stem: A ward is caring for a patient with COVID-19 who is not undergoing any aerosol-generating procedures.
questions.leadIn: Which PPE set fits routine care?
options: Gown, gloves and eye protection with a mask
No PPE once the patient is afebrile
questions.explanation: First Aid lists **gown, gloves and eye protection** for staff caring for COVID-19 patients; a mask covers droplet spread at close range (Davidson: surgical mask for close contact). An **N95** becomes mandatory only for aerosol-generating procedures.
whyNot: Gloves alone do not protect the face or airway.
Spread is not tied to fever, and pre-symptomatic shedding occurs.
Lead aprons are radiation protection.
A sterile gown is not the recommended PPE set.

questions.stem: A student compares the three severe human coronaviruses.
questions.leadIn: Which statement about SARS-CoV-2 is correct?
options: It is more transmissible but less lethal per case than SARS-CoV
It has a higher case-fatality than MERS-CoV
It mainly spreads by the faecal–oral route
Its animal reservoir is proven to be the dromedary camel
questions.explanation: SARS-CoV-2 is **clearly more transmissible** than SARS-CoV but **less lethal** (early estimate 1–5%, versus ~10% for SARS and ~35% for MERS).
whyNot: MERS has the highest mortality, about 35%.
It spreads via respiratory droplets/particles.
Coronaviruses are RNA viruses.
Camels are the source of MERS-CoV; the SARS-CoV-2 reservoir is uncertain.

questions.stem: A public-health lecture covers who should receive COVID-19 vaccination.
questions.leadIn: Which group does Step-Up highlight as particularly important to vaccinate?
options: Older patients and those with significant comorbidities
Only people who have already had COVID-19
questions.explanation: Vaccination is indicated for all patients, **especially the elderly and those with significant comorbidities**, and sits alongside influenza and pneumococcal vaccines for pneumonia prevention.
whyNot: Health workers are vaccinated, but the recommendation is far wider.
Recommendations cover all ages from 6 months, not just young children.
Previous infection is not the criterion.
Travel is not the basis of the recommendation.

questions.stem: A 69-year-old man with type 2 diabetes and obesity has 5 days of fever, cough and loss of smell. Today he is breathless; saturation is 90% on air. Bloods: lymphocytes 0.6 × 10⁹/L, platelets 120 × 10⁹/L, raised D-dimer and LDH. Chest X-ray shows bilateral peripheral opacities.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Step 1, the history: fever and cough with **anosmia** point to COVID-19. Step 2, the risk profile: **age, diabetes and obesity** predict severe disease, and he is now hypoxic (the "severe" tier). Step 3, the labs: **lymphopenia** (the commonest abnormality), **thrombocytopenia**, raised **D-dimer** and **LDH** fit. Step 4, the imaging: **bilateral, peripheral** opacities are typical. Together these make **COVID-19 pneumonia** the answer; confirm with nasopharyngeal RT-PCR.
whyNot: Pneumococcal pneumonia gives lobar, usually unilateral consolidation and a neutrophilia, and no anosmia.
TB is subacute with weight loss and upper-lobe changes.
LVF causes bilateral changes but not fever, anosmia or lymphopenia.
PCP occurs in the immunocompromised (e.g. advanced HIV); nothing suggests that here.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old woman with COVID-19 is admitted with saturation of 88% on air and needs 2 L/min of nasal oxygen. She is not ventilated. Her eGFR is normal.
questions.leadIn: Which treatment plan fits best?
options: Dexamethasone with or without remdesivir, plus anticoagulation
questions.explanation: Step 1, place her on the ladder: she is **hospitalised and needs supplemental oxygen**. Step 2, that tier means **dexamethasone ± remdesivir**; dexamethasone is the drug that lowers 28-day mortality in oxygen-requiring patients. Step 3, every admitted patient needs **anticoagulation** because of the high thrombosis rate, at a prophylactic or therapeutic dose depending on risk. Step 4, IL-6 or JAK blockade is kept for ventilated patients or rapidly rising oxygen needs.
whyNot: She is hypoxic and needs admission; home care is for mild disease.
Oral antivirals are for high-risk patients who are not in hospital.
IL-6 blockers are added to dexamethasone in ventilated or rapidly worsening patients, not used alone.
Antibiotics do not treat the virus.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man arrives in the emergency department with fever, cough and hypoxia. COVID-19 is suspected while results are awaited, and he may need intubation.
questions.leadIn: Which infection-control approach is most appropriate?
options: Isolate him and use gown, gloves, eye protection and an N95 respirator for aerosol-generating procedures, with strict hand hygiene
Nurse him in an open bay with standard precautions only
Wait for a positive PCR before any precautions
Use a surgical mask for intubation
questions.explanation: Step 1, assume infectivity: early symptoms are non-specific and pre-symptomatic spread happens, so precautions start on suspicion, not on the result. Step 2, isolate the patient. Step 3, PPE: **gown, gloves and eye protection**, and an **N95** for **aerosol-generating procedures** such as intubation. Step 4, **hand hygiene** before and after every contact, the single most important IPC measure.
whyNot: Standard precautions in an open bay risk spread to other patients.
Waiting for the result exposes staff and patients during the delay.
A surgical mask does not protect against aerosols.
Antibiotics do not prevent viral infection.

questions.theme: Diagnosis and monitoring tests in suspected COVID-19
questions.leadIn: Match each patient below to the single best option in the list. Any option can be the answer to one item, to several items, or to none.
options: Rapid antigen test of the anterior nares

items.stem: A 40-year-old woman with fever, cough and loss of taste needs the single most sensitive test to confirm SARS-CoV-2 infection.
items.explanation: **RT-PCR (NAAT)** on a **nasopharyngeal** swab is the most sensitive and reliable test.

items.stem: A school wants a quick point-of-care test so a coughing pupil can be told to isolate the same day, accepting lower sensitivity.
items.explanation: **Rapid antigen testing** gives an immediate result to allow early isolation, at the cost of sensitivity.

items.stem: A 63-year-old man with COVID-19 has an equivocal chest X-ray, and the team wants imaging that will show bilateral peripheral ground-glass change if present.
items.explanation: **CT chest** shows the peripheral ground-glass opacities and is advised when the diagnosis is uncertain.

items.stem: A 70-year-old admitted with COVID-19: the team wants the blood test most likely to show the commonest lab abnormality of the disease.
items.explanation: The **full blood count** shows **lymphopenia**, the commonest laboratory abnormality (often with thrombocytopenia).

questions.theme: Treatment choices across the COVID-19 severity spectrum
questions.leadIn: Match each patient below to the single best option in the list. Any option can be the answer to one item, to several items, or to none.
options: Home isolation and symptom relief only
Oral antiviral such as Paxlovid or molnupiravir

items.stem: A fit 24-year-old with 2 days of sore throat, fever and positive PCR, saturation 98% on air.
items.explanation: Mild disease in a low-risk patient is managed at **home** with isolation, monitoring and symptom relief.

items.stem: A 71-year-old with CKD and diabetes has mild COVID-19, saturation 96% on air, and is not admitted.
items.explanation: Not hospitalised but **high risk** of severe disease: an oral antiviral (or neutralising antibody) is used.

items.stem: A 68-year-old admitted with COVID-19 pneumonia needs 3 L/min of oxygen.
A 59-year-old already on dexamethasone for COVID-19 deteriorates and is intubated in ICU.
items.explanation: Ventilated (or rapidly rising oxygen need): dexamethasone **plus an IL-6 blocker** such as tocilizumab (or a JAK inhibitor).

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man recovering from COVID-19 develops tingling in his feet followed over 5 days by symmetrical leg weakness rising to his hips. Reflexes are absent.
questions.leadIn: Which complication is most likely?
options: Spinal cord compression from a metastasis
questions.explanation: Ascending symmetrical weakness with **areflexia** after a viral illness is **Guillain–Barré syndrome**; COVID-19 is listed among its viral triggers.
whyNot: Stroke is a recognised COVID complication but gives sudden, usually one-sided deficits with brisk reflexes later.
Cord compression causes a sensory level and later upper motor neurone signs.
Myasthenia causes fatigable weakness with preserved reflexes.
Periodic paralysis is episodic and linked to potassium, not ascending sensory symptoms.

questions.stem: An infection-control nurse is explaining how respiratory viruses reach new patients on a ward. She points to a door handle and a shared ultrasound probe.
questions.leadIn: What is the term for these objects in transmission?
questions.explanation: Inanimate objects such as door handles, taps and ultrasound probes that carry pathogens between patients are **fomites**, especially linked to health care–associated infection.
whyNot: Vectors are living, e.g. mosquitoes or fleas.
A reservoir is where the organism normally lives and multiplies.
A carrier is an infected person or animal, not an object.
An index case is the first identified patient in an outbreak.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man who completed his COVID-19 vaccination course develops a mild cough and positive antigen test. He recovers at home within a week. He says the vaccine "failed".
questions.leadIn: Which statement best answers him?
options: Breakthrough infection is expected; the vaccine mainly reduces severity
The vaccine was clearly given incorrectly
Vaccines protect only against bacterial pneumonia
He should be given a live attenuated vaccine instead
Infection after vaccination means he is immunodeficient
questions.explanation: COVID-19 vaccines are highly effective but act mainly by **reducing severity**; **breakthrough infection** still occurs and is usually much milder, as here.
whyNot: Mild breakthrough infection does not imply a technique error.
COVID-19 vaccines target the viral spike protein.
There is no reason to switch; live vaccines also carry risks in the immunocompromised.
Breakthrough infection is common and does not by itself suggest immunodeficiency.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man with COVID-19 on ICU has AKI. Renal biopsy shows a collapsing pattern of glomerular injury. Genetic testing shows a high-risk APOL1 genotype.
questions.leadIn: What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: COVID-19 is a recognised viral cause of **secondary FSGS**, typically the **collapsing** variant in people with a **high-risk APOL1 genotype**; ATN remains the more common AKI lesion overall.
whyNot: ATN is commoner but is a tubular, not glomerular collapsing, lesion.
IgA nephropathy shows mesangial IgA deposits.
Minimal change shows normal glomeruli on light microscopy.
Anti-GBM disease is a crescentic GN with linear IgG.

questions.stem: A 36-year-old woman was exposed to a colleague with COVID-19 eleven days ago. She now has fever and cough.
questions.leadIn: How should the timing be interpreted?
options: It is within the incubation period, so COVID-19 is possible
It is too long after exposure for COVID-19
It is too short for COVID-19, which takes at least 3 weeks
Only symptoms within 24 hours of exposure are relevant
Incubation is irrelevant because COVID-19 is always asymptomatic
questions.explanation: The incubation of SARS-CoV-2 runs **up to 14 days** (average about 5), so symptoms on day 11 still fit.
whyNot: Day 11 is inside the 2–14 day window.
Incubation is usually around 5 days, not weeks.
Symptoms within 24 hours would be unusually early.
Many infections are symptomatic; illness ranges from none to critical.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old man returns from the Arabian Peninsula, where he visited a camel farm and drank raw camel milk. Ten days later he develops fever, cough, diarrhoea and rapidly worsening respiratory failure.
questions.leadIn: Which coronavirus is most likely?
questions.explanation: Camel contact in the **Arabian Peninsula**, prominent diarrhoea and rapid respiratory failure in an older man point to **MERS-CoV**, a zoonosis passing from bats to camels to humans, with about 35% mortality.
whyNot: SARS-CoV-2 spreads person to person and has no established camel link.
229E causes the common cold.
OC43 causes the common cold.
SARS-CoV has not caused natural infection since 2003.

questions.stem: A clinician diagnoses COVID-19 in a 48-year-old patient during a pandemic and asks about legal duties.
questions.leadIn: What is the correct action?
options: Notify the public-health authorities, as COVID-19 is a reportable disease
Notify only if the patient dies
Notify only with the patient’s written consent
No notification is needed for viral infections
Report only to the patient’s employer
questions.explanation: COVID-19 is a **reportable (notifiable) infectious disease**; clinicians have a duty to notify public-health officials.
whyNot: Notification applies to cases, not only deaths.
Statutory notification does not depend on consent.
Many viral diseases are notifiable, including SARS and MERS.
Employers are not the public-health authority.

ospe.identify: CT chest in COVID-19 pneumonia: dense bilateral lower-lobe opacities with air bronchograms (typical pattern is bilateral, peripheral, posterior lower-lobe change).
WHO hand-washing technique: name the steps and the commonly missed areas (fingertips, web spaces, palmar creases, backs of hands); a full wash takes 40–60 seconds.
